name: Disorders Caused by Venomous Snakebites and Marine Animal Exposures

clinicalPearls: Medically important venomous snakes fall into Viperidae (Old World vipers and New World/Asian pit vipers), Elapidae (cobras, kraits, coral snakes, sea snakes, Australian elapids), the burrowing asps (Atractaspidinae), and a few colubrids; snake envenomation is described as the world's deadliest neglected tropical disease, with roughly 63,000 deaths globally in 2019.
A large fraction of bites are 'dry' (no venom injected) - about 20-25% of pit viper bites and up to 75% of sea snake bites - so the presence of fang marks alone does not equal envenomation.

Viperid/cytotoxic patterns produce progressive local pain, soft-tissue swelling, ecchymosis, and hemorrhagic or serum-filled blisters, while neurotoxic elapids (kraits, some cobras, Australian elapids) and certain vipers cause cranial nerve dysfunction (ptosis, dysphagia) progressing to descending paralysis and respiratory failure.

Onset and tempo of symptoms vary with species, bite location, and venom dose; coral snakes, sea snakes, and some non-North American vipers (e.g., hump-nosed pit viper) can have systemic effects delayed by several hours, mandating prolonged observation.

In resource-limited settings the bedside 20-minute whole-blood clotting test detects venom-induced coagulopathy: 1-2 mL venous blood left undisturbed in a clean dry glass tube that fails to clot at 20 minutes indicates coagulopathy.

Antivenom binds and neutralizes circulating (unbound) venom; it is largely ineffective at reversing damage already established (e.g., fixed paralysis, established renal failure) and offers little cross-protection outside the species it was raised against, so species-appropriate selection is essential.

Compartment syndrome is uncommon after snakebite (fasciotomy needed in under 1% of cases); in North American crotalid bites fasciotomy lacks supporting evidence and may increase morbidity, since effective antivenom lowers compartment pressure.

Recurrent or delayed coagulopathy can appear during the first 2-3 weeks after a bite because venom antigens may outlast antivenom, so patients are warned to avoid elective surgery/high-trauma activity and to have repeat coagulation testing.

Long-term sequelae include permanent limb functional loss from muscle/nerve/vascular injury or scar contracture, and pituitary insufficiency described after Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) envenomation.

Among marine animals, jellyfish/box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri), Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia), and the Irukandji jellyfish (Carukia barnesi) cause the most dangerous cnidarian stings; Irukandji syndrome is a catecholamine-excess state with hypertension, tachycardia, severe pain, and risk of pulmonary edema and cardiomyopathy.

Blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) and pufferfish (order Tetraodontiformes, e.g., fugu) both cause tetrodotoxin toxicity - a sodium-channel blocker producing rapid flaccid paralysis with preserved mentation; consciousness is typically intact even during complete paralysis, so analgesia/sedation matter.

Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning mimics an allergic reaction (flushing, urticaria, headache, palpitations) and arises when bacteria decarboxylate histidine to histamine in poorly refrigerated fish; the toxin is heat-stable and reactions are more severe in patients on isoniazid (histaminase blockade).

Ciguatera, caused by heat-stable ciguatoxins (Gambierdiscus toxicus) bioaccumulated in large reef fish, classically produces GI symptoms plus neurologic features including reversal of hot/cold temperature sensation and a sensation of 'loose teeth'; neurologic symptoms can persist for weeks.
harrison.pathophysiology: Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes, polypeptides, and glycoproteins whose composition varies by species, age, diet, geography, and even within a species. They produce harm through several mechanisms: direct local tissue necrosis, disruption of the coagulation cascade at multiple steps (consumptive coagulopathy, defibrination, thrombocytopenia), organ dysfunction (notably renal), and action at the neuromuscular junction causing paralysis. Early hypotension is partly mediated by bradykinin-potentiating factors causing vasodilation and pooling, compounded by systemic bleeding, hemolysis, and third-spacing of intravascular volume. Renal injury is usually acute tubular necrosis (often reversible), but bilateral cortical necrosis carries a poorer prognosis. Marine envenomations operate by distinct toxins: cnidarian nematocysts inject venom containing phospholipases, metalloproteases, pore-forming toxins, neurotoxins, and bioactive amines (histamine, serotonin); cone snail conotoxins block acetylcholine receptors and ion channels; blue-ringed octopus and pufferfish deliver tetrodotoxin, a potent peripheral sodium-channel blocker. Marine seafood poisonings are ingestion toxidromes: scombroid from bacterial conversion of histidine to histamine in spoiled fish, and ciguatera from ciguatoxins that activate neuronal sodium channels and antagonize voltage-gated potassium channels.
additionalDifferentials: Nonvenomous snakebite or 'dry' bite (fang marks without envenomation)
Bite by a harmless species whose saliva causes mild local pain/edema (can mimic mild envenomation)
Cellulitis or other local soft-tissue infection
Allergic reaction / anaphylaxis (especially scombroid, which mimics food allergy)
Ciguatera differential per Harrison: paralytic shellfish poisoning, eosinophilic meningitis, type E botulism, organophosphate poisoning, tetrodotoxin poisoning, psychogenic hyperventilation
infectionMimics: Cellulitis (rapidly spreading local swelling and erythema after a bite can resemble bacterial cellulitis)
Secondary bacterial wound infection complicating an envenomation (marine wounds: Vibrio in saltwater, Aeromonas in freshwater; Staphylococcus/Streptococcus)
nonInfectiousMimics: Anaphylaxis to venom or to antivenom itself
Compartment syndrome from other causes of limb swelling/trauma
Primary cardiac dysrhythmia or shock from non-toxic causes
Acute neuromuscular paralysis from other etiologies (e.g., botulism, Guillain-Barre) when neurotoxic envenomation presents with descending weakness
additionalInvestigations: Complete blood count (assess hemorrhage, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia)
Coagulation studies: prothrombin time and fibrinogen level; fibrin degradation products / D-dimer
Creatine kinase for suspected rhabdomyolysis; urine for blood/myoglobin
20-minute whole-blood clotting test where laboratory access is limited
Serial limb circumference measurements at three points every 15 min until local effects stabilize
ECG and chest radiography in severe envenomation or significant comorbidity
Intracompartmental pressure measurement if compartment syndrome suspected (threshold 30-40 mmHg)
Imaging (soft-tissue radiography, ultrasound, or MRI) to locate retained marine spines/foreign bodies
Repeat coagulation and CBC monitoring for recurrent coagulopathy after discharge
redFlags: Bite to the face or neck (risk of rapid airway-threatening swelling)
Cranial nerve signs such as ptosis or difficulty swallowing (herald impending respiratory compromise in neurotoxic envenomation)
Rapidly progressing swelling involving more than half the bitten limb, extensive blistering/bruising, or severe pain
Spontaneous systemic bleeding, hemolysis, or laboratory evidence of coagulopathy
Hypotension or shock unresponsive to fluids
Rhabdomyolysis with falling urine output / acute renal failure
Irukandji syndrome features: severe hypertension, chest/abdominal pain, then risk of pulmonary edema and cardiomyopathy
Tetrodotoxin exposure (blue-ringed octopus, pufferfish): oral/facial numbness progressing to flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure
harrison.prognosis: In settings with rapid access to care and appropriate antivenom, mortality is low - under 1% in the United States among victims who receive antivenom. Eastern and western diamondback rattlesnakes account for most U.S. snakebite deaths; globally, major killers include cobras, saw-scaled/carpet vipers (Echis), Russell's vipers, large African vipers (Bitis), lanceheads (Bothrops), and tropical rattlesnakes (Crotalus durissus). Morbidity from permanent limb functional loss is substantial and can be devastating in the developing world; in the U.S. it is more common and severe after rattlesnake bites than after copperhead or water moccasin bites. Renal failure from acute tubular necrosis is frequently reversible, whereas bilateral cortical necrosis carries a worse renal prognosis. For tetrodotoxin/blue-ringed octopus envenomation, recovery usually occurs within 24-48 h and long-term sequelae are uncommon unless hypoxia/hypoperfusion supervened. Most scombroid cases are mild and self-limited (resolving in 8-12 h), and ciguatera GI symptoms typically settle in 24-48 h though neurologic symptoms may persist for days to weeks (and a delayed 'second-phase' syndrome can last 2-6 weeks after parrotfish exposure).
pitfalls: Treating fang marks alone as proof of envenomation - many bites are dry and antivenom in such cases is useless and potentially harmful.
Relying on color pattern, head shape, or pupil shape to judge whether a snake is venomous - nonvenomous species frequently mimic these features.

Discharging a patient too early: significant toxicity from an apparently 'dry' viperid bite can develop after several hours, and elapid/sea snake/some viper systemic effects are characteristically delayed.

Using outdated first aid (incision, suction, tourniquets/venom-sequestration devices) - these worsen local damage and increase infection risk; pressure-immobilization is reserved for reliably identified primarily neurotoxic species, not viperids.
Relying on antivenom skin testing for hypersensitivity - it is neither sensitive nor specific; prophylactic antihistamines/glucocorticoids have not proven beneficial.
Performing fasciotomy reflexively for limb swelling in North American crotalid bites - evidence does not support it and it may increase morbidity.
Giving blood products before adequate antivenom - this can fuel ongoing consumptive coagulopathy.

In marine cnidarian stings, applying vinegar indiscriminately - it relieves pain for Indo-Pacific species (C. fleckeri, C. barnesi) but can increase nematocyst discharge in Physalia physalis and Chrysaora quinquecirrha; rubbing the area also worsens stinging.
Mislabeling scombroid poisoning as a seafood allergy, leading to unnecessary lifelong fish avoidance.
Using beta-blockers in Irukandji syndrome hypertension - risks worsening hypertension via unopposed alpha effects.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison grades pit viper envenomation severity (U.S./Canada framework) as: None - fang marks only ('dry' bite); Mild - local findings only (pain, ecchymosis, nonprogressive swelling); Moderate - clearly progressing swelling, systemic symptoms/signs, and/or laboratory abnormalities; Severe - neurologic dysfunction, respiratory distress, and/or cardiovascular instability/shock.
management: Give species-appropriate intravenous antivenom as the mainstay for systemic envenomation, with adrenaline, antihistamine, and corticosteroid on standby for anaphylaxis
Apply first aid by immobilising the bitten limb near heart level and removing constricting items, while avoiding incision, suction, and arterial tourniquets
Resuscitate supportively: protect the airway and provide mechanical ventilation for neurotoxic paralysis, and give intravenous fluids for hypotension
Correct venom-induced coagulopathy by repeating antivenom guided by the whole-blood clotting test and transfusing blood products for active haemorrhage
Manage acute kidney injury from tubular necrosis with renal replacement therapy where needed, and treat rhabdomyolysis
For anticholinesterase-responsive postsynaptic neurotoxicity give an anticholinesterase such as neostigmine with atropine
Provide wound care with tetanus prophylaxis, reserving debridement or fasciotomy for genuine necrosis or compartment syndrome
For marine envenomation use hot-water immersion for stingray and stonefish stings, vinegar for box jellyfish, and stonefish antivenom where indicated
